title: Tesla FSD için Almanya'dan yeşil ışık: İsim değişikliği gündemde
summary: Alman düzenleyiciler Tesla'nın Full Self-Driving teknolojisinin Avrupa çapında onaylanmasını destekliyor ancak isminin değiştirilmesini istiyor.
body:
Alman ulaştırma makamları, Tesla'nın Full Self-Driving (FSD) teknolojisinin Avrupa Birliği genelinde onaylanmasını desteklediklerini açıkladı. InsideEVs'in aktardığına göre, Almanya Ulaştırma Bakanlığı ile Tesla arasında eylül ayında yapılan görüşmeler sonucunda teknik ve sorumluluk konularında uzlaşıya varıldı. Bakanlık, sistemin Avrupa çapında onaylanması için girişimde bulunacağını duyurdu.

## İsim değişikliği ve hız sınırı düzenlemesi

Alman düzenleyiciler, "Full Self-Driving" yani "Tam Olarak Kendiliğinden Sürüş" ifadesinin sürücüleri yanıltabileceğini belirterek bu ismin değiştirilmesini talep etti. Sürücülerin sorumluluğun kendilerinde olduğunu açıkça göstermek amacıyla Tesla'nın bu sistemi "Tesla Assisted Driving" olarak adlandırmayı teklif ettiği bildirildi. Ayrıca taraflar, trafik akışını rahatlatmak amacıyla hız sınırının yüzde 10 üzerine kadar çıkılmasına izin verilmesi konusunda anlaştı. ABD versiyonunda bulunan ve aşırı hız yapabilen "Mad Max" modunun ise Avrupa versiyonunda yer almadığı belirtiliyor.

## Avrupa'daki yayılım ve güvenlik tartışmaları

FSD teknolojisi halihazırda Hollanda, Belçika, Danimarka, Litvanya, Estonya, Slovenya, Çekya ve Hırvatistan'da sürücüler tarafından kullanılabiliyor. Teslarati'nin aktardığı bilgilere göre, Tesla güvenlik odaklı paylaşımlarına devam ederken sistemin kavşaklarda ani tehlikeleri önleyebildiğini gösteren yeni görüntüler de kamuoyuyla paylaşıldı. Öte yandan, AB genelindeki resmi oylamanın aralık ayına ertelendiği ifade ediliyor.

**Neden önemli?** Almanya'nın desteği, FSD teknolojisinin Avrupa Birliği genelindeki diğer ülkelere yayılma sürecini hızlandırabilir ve gelecekteki düzenleyici kararlar için kritik bir referans oluşturabilir.

source_texts.title: Tesla FSD Just Got The Green Light From Germany. But It Might Need A New Name
source_texts.summary: German regulators support approving FSD for use throughout Europe. But they want Tesla to drop the "Full Self Driving" name.
source_texts.text:
Tesla FSD Just Got The Green Light From Germany. But It Might Need A New Name
German regulators support approving FSD for use throughout Europe. But they want Tesla to drop the "Full Self Driving" name.
- German regulators support EU-wide FSD approval with a speed offset capped at 10% above the limit.
- Tesla has offered to rename FSD “Tesla Assisted Driving” to make clear that drivers remain fully responsible, the statement claims.
- FSD is available in eight European countries, but EU-wide approval remains pending.
An October 6 statement from Germany’s Federal Ministry of Transport details September talks between Transport Minister Steffen Bilger and Tesla about the future of its "Full Self-Driving" technology suite. They reached agreement on technical and liability issues, prompting Bilger to push for timely EU-wide approval, the office announced.
The ministry says they agreed to allow speeds up to 10% above the limit, conceding that small excesses can sometimes smooth traffic flow. That tackles a major concern regulators had about excessive speeding, as the U.S. version of FSD includes a "Mad Max" mode that drives far over the speed limit in some circumstances.
Regulators were also concerned about the technology's long-controversial name. German regulators consider the FSD name to be misleading. Tesla will reportedly address this by calling it “Tesla Assisted Driving” instead, according to the German account of the discussion.
The ministry praises the system’s urban capabilities, too, but still has some criticism for Tesla. The statement notes that the system still doesn't require any driver intervention to handle steering, acceleration, and braking, which could create confusion. In general, the statement is supporting European regulatory approval for the tech, not actually approving its current form.
FSD’s European rollout has been a patchwork, but approval in Germany might smooth adoption throughout the rest of the European Union. When it debuted in the Netherlands in April, the decision to allow it on public roads followed more than 18 months of assessment. Other countries can recognize that authorization individually, while EU-wide acceptance requires a separate vote by member states.
FSD also differs between the U.S. and Europe. One difference is how the speed offset feature works, and another is that the European version approved by Dutch regulators excludes the more aggressive ‘Mad Max’ driving mode available in the U.S.
Early FSD demonstrations in Europe have put it in a very positive light. It had no trouble navigating incredibly tight cobbled streets in downtown Aarhus, Denmark, where cyclists, pedestrians and cafe customers left precious little room for a car to pass. The drive showed impressive spatial judgment with only minor mistakes.
FSD passed 1.48 million subscribers in July. It introduced FSD subscriptions in the U.S. in July 2021, initially charging $199 a month alongside an outright purchase option. In February 2026, it dropped the upfront purchase for new U.S. customers, making FSD subscription-only. Today, it costs $99 a month in the U.S. and €99 in European markets.
Drivers already have access in the Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark, Lithuania, Estonia, Slovenia, the Czech Republic, and Croatia. With Germany now supporting wider approval, how much longer will it take for FSD to spread to the rest of Europe?

source_texts.title: Tesla FSD changed its mind mid-intersection, and it may have saved a life
source_texts.summary: Tesla shares dashcam footage of FSD Supervised stopping mid intersection to avoid a T-bone crash. The post Tesla FSD changed its mind mid-intersection, and it may have saved a life appeared first on TESLARATI .
source_texts.text:
Tesla is putting another Full Self-Driving save in front of its 24.8 million followers on X.
On Tuesday morning, Tesla’s main account shared a dashcam clip with the caption “FSD Supervised preventing T-bone crash.” The footage came from an owner posting as TheNewGrid, who described what happened at a stop sign: “I looked at the car coming to the stop sign figured they would stop, my car went, then came to a stop mid intersection as they flew by. Had I been manually driving this would have resulted in a crash.”
The sequence is the notable part. FSD had already started crossing when the other driver ran the stop sign. Instead of pressing on, the car braked hard in the middle of the intersection and let the crossing vehicle pass in front of it. By the owner’s own account, they had made the same assumption the software initially made, that the other car would stop, and would not have corrected in time.
FSD Supervised preventing T-bone crash
— Tesla (@Tesla) October 6, 2026
The clip is the latest in a run of safety posts Tesla has amplified over the past several days. On Saturday, the company shared a video from Selling Sunset star Jason Oppenheim, who sold his Bentley for a Model Y and said he was buying Teslas with FSD for 10 of his employees. Ashok Elluswamy, who leads Tesla AI, followed up by writing that Tesla self-driving “reacts to other people cutting into your path with super-human response times.” On Monday, a Cybertruck owner posted footage of FSD moving across three lanes from a red light to clear a path for an ambulance approaching from behind.
This recent clip also lands a few weeks after Tesla began shipping Automatic Collision Evasion with FSD v14.3.9, a feature that can activate FSD on the driver’s behalf when a frontal collision is imminent or the driver appears distracted. Elluswamy said in September that “even earlier prediction of hazards, even faster reaction time and overall significantly better safety and collision avoidance” are coming with v15, the release Tesla has tied to round the clock Robotaxi operation.
The safety messaging matters beyond social media. Tesla has said FSD Supervised was 4.1 times less likely to crash than manual driving across 100 million kilometers on European roads, and it has been putting those figures in front of regulators. Eight EU countries have now approved FSD Supervised, with Croatia the most recent, but the EU’s bloc-wide vote originally set for October 6 has been pushed to December at the earliest.
FSD Supervised is still a Level 2 system, and the driver remains responsible at all times. Even heavy users find reasons to step in. Teslarati’s Joey Klender, who uses FSD for about 76 percent of his driving, laid out five recurring issues on Tuesday that still prompt him to intervene. Clips like this one show the other column of that ledger: moments where the software caught a mistake a human was about to make.
